title: Document comments: the decisions before the real build

steps.path: Any file open in the file viewer, in Comments mode
steps.headline: Where should your comments be saved?
steps.today: The comments in the preview live only in memory. Close the preview and they are gone.
steps.problem: Real comments have to be saved somewhere, and where decides what happens when you move, copy or back up a file.
steps.proposal: Three places they could be saved. None of them changes how comments look or work in the app.

options.label: Hidden folder in the project
options.summary: One hidden comments folder inside each project folder, next to the app's other hidden project data.
pros: Nothing new appears among your files.
Copy or back up the project folder and its comments come along.
The easiest one to upload to your account later, when sharing comes.
cons: Moving one file to a different project leaves its comments behind (they show as "file not found" rather than vanishing silently).
Files opened from outside any project need a fallback place, which would be the app's own folder.

options.label: A file beside each document
options.summary: Commenting on notes.md creates notes.md.comments next to it.
pros: Comments travel with the file wherever you copy it.
Anyone opening the folder can see a file has comments.
cons: A second file appears next to every document you comment on, cluttering your folders.
Rename or move the document in another program and the pair splits.

options.label: The app's own folder
options.summary: All comments in one place inside YouCoded's settings folder, never in your projects.
pros: Your project folders never change at all.
cons: Copying or backing up a project does not carry its comments.
Another computer never sees them until sync exists.

steps.path: Comments sent with Ask Your Assistant, or the assistant reading a file
steps.headline: What may the assistant do with comments? Pick all that apply.
steps.today: The assistant cannot see comments at all yet. Ask Your Assistant only sends them as pills in a message.
steps.problem: You wanted the assistant to act on your markup and to resolve comments, but each thing it may do is something that happens without you pressing a button.
steps.proposal: Every action the assistant takes shows its name on the comment and appears under Show Resolved, so nothing it does is hidden. Pick what it is allowed to do.

options.label: Reply to comments
pros: Answers a question right under it, where you asked it.
cons: More replies to read in busy documents.

options.label: Resolve comments
pros: After fixing what you asked, it closes the comment for you.
cons: It could close one you think is not done; you reopen it with one click.

options.label: Leave its own comments
pros: It can review a document the way a colleague would, with notes pinned to the exact lines.
cons: A long document could collect many notes you did not ask for.

options.label: Edit the file to fix what a comment asks
options.summary: Follows the same approval rules the assistant already has for editing files.
pros: "Reword this" gets reworded, not just discussed.
cons: Edits can move text a comment points at; a comment whose words disappear shows as "text no longer found".

steps.path: The file viewer on the phone app
steps.headline: Should comments work on the phone in this first version?
steps.today: The phone app shows files with the same screens as desktop, but phones have no hover, so hovering a highlight to read it does not exist there.
steps.problem: Building phone support now makes the first version bigger. Leaving it out means comments you make on desktop look different or missing on the phone.
steps.proposal: Two ways to do it now, or leave it for later.

options.label: Now: tap opens the list
options.summary: Tapping a highlight opens the comment list on that comment, the same as clicking on desktop. Selecting text shows Add comment.
pros: Same behaviour as desktop, so one thing to learn.
Most of the screens are already shared, so the extra work is mainly saving on the phone and testing by touch.
cons: Just reading one comment takes the full list, since there is no quick peek.
The first version takes longer.

options.label: Now: tap shows a bubble
options.summary: The first tap shows the comment in a small bubble (the phone's version of hover); a second tap opens the list.
pros: A quick read without leaving the document.
cons: Two taps to reply, and people often miss that a second tap does something.
The first version takes longer.

options.label: Later
options.summary: The phone shows highlights and nothing else until a follow-up.
pros: The desktop version arrives sooner.
cons: On the phone you see highlighted text you cannot open, which looks broken.

steps.path: Word documents (.docx) opened in the file viewer
steps.headline: What should happen with comments on Word documents in this first version?
steps.today: The file viewer shows Word documents read-only, and it drops any comments already in them. Nothing in the app writes Word files.
steps.problem: Real Word comments, the kind Word and Google Docs both see, need the app to write Word files, which it has never done. A mistake there could damage a document.

options.label: Comment in the app only
options.summary: You can comment on a Word document like any other file, but the comments stay in YouCoded. Writing them into the Word file comes later.
pros: Word documents work like every other file from day one.
Your Word files are never changed, so nothing can be damaged.
cons: Open the file in Word and your YouCoded comments are not there (yet).

options.label: Also show Word's own comments
options.summary: As above, plus comments someone already left in Word appear, read-only.
pros: You see what a colleague wrote in Word.
cons: Two kinds of comments on one file, and only one kind can be replied to.
More work in the first version.

options.label: No comments on Word files yet
pros: Smallest first version.
cons: Right-click on a Word document offers Ask about this but not Add comment, which is inconsistent.

steps.path: Draft pull request #263 on the app's GitHub page
steps.headline: Close the July "Ask Claude about this" draft (#263) without merging it?
steps.today: The July attempt is still an open draft on GitHub. You decided to drop it, and its plan is already archived.
steps.problem: An open draft looks like live work to anyone, including future assistant sessions, and closing it shows on GitHub.
steps.proposal: Yes closes it with a note pointing to this work; the code stays on GitHub and can be reopened. No leaves it open.

options.label: Close it
pros: Nobody mistakes it for current work.
cons: None; it can be reopened.

options.label: Leave it open
pros: Nothing changes on GitHub.
cons: Two competing versions of the same feature appear open.
